item.title: 'Bold creativity', but 'certification remains crucial': Chinese auto industry leaders react to Tesla's 'flying car' Roadster
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17 14:15:00
A photo of the Roadster Photo: Tesla US tech giant Tesla held an event at a SpaceX rocket test site on Thursday US time and officially unveiled its second-generation Roadster, which has been widely described as a "flying car," drawing considerable attention from China, with many Chinese auto industry leaders commending the innovation. Notably, the car is also open for reservations in China, though actual delivery plans remain unclear. Video footage of the demonstration has been widely shared on Chinese social media, and many also turned their attention to how Chinese auto executives view the "flying" Roadster. Li Bin, Chinese electric vehicle (EV) maker NIO's founder, chairman and CEO, reposted a link to Tesla's demonstration video of Roadster on Sina Weibo and commented: "This is incredible! We really don't have this - thumbs up for Tesla." The comment appears to be a nod to a previous remark made by Li. The NIO founder once declared that "whatever Tesla has, I have; and what I have, Tesla doesn't." Now, as Tesla's Roadster sparks heated discussion, Li's remarks from eight years ago have been dug up again and quickly become a viral internet meme, according to some auto industry news outlets. He Xiaopeng, chairman of EV maker XPENG, said in a post on WeChat that the Roadster represents "a very cool alternative form of a flying car," according to several media reports. He added that whether the product can be realized depends on flight safety, performance parameters, range, and crucially, flight certification. He noted that these requirements require long-term efforts both in China and the US and expressed hope that progress can accelerate. Zhao Deli, founder of XPENG AEROHT (ARIDGE), the flying car affiliate of XPENG and the first company in China to mass-produce a flying car, said the demonstration showcased "bold creativity" and vector-control technology. "This helps more people believe in the future of flying cars," said Zhao. In a livestream of the demonstration on Thursday local time, Tesla demonstrated additional capabilities. The Roadster slowly followed a C-shaped suspended track, hovered while oriented vertically relative to the ground, and remained suspended at the top parallel surface of the track. After accelerating off the upper end of the track, the vehicle adjusted the direction of its thrusters mid-air to perform a 180-degree flip before landing smoothly. According to Tesla's official website, the Roadster is offered in three versions - Performance, Thrust and Rocket. All three are listed with an estimated range of approximately 300 miles (483 kilometers) and a top speed exceeding 230 mph (370 kilometers per hour). In the US, reservations are open for the Performance version with a deposit of $50,000 and the Thrust version with a deposit of $250,000. The Rocket version is available by invitation only. Tesla's China website currently accepts reservations only for the Performance version, with a fully refundable deposit of 332,000 yuan ($49,653). The site notes that whether the vehicle can ultimately be sold in a given market will depend on applicable local laws and regulations at the time of launch. Tesla CEO Elon Musk stated that production of the Roadster is scheduled to begin in 2028. According to previous reports, the original Roadster was first delivered in 2008 at a price of about $100,000 and was discontinued in 2012. Tesla announced plans for a new Roadster in 2017 with a target delivery date of 2020, but the project has faced repeated delays. Global Times

item.title: Apple's iPhone Duo pre-orders sell out in seconds in China, with some deliveries delayed until next year
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17 14:03:00
An Apple store in Beijing Photo: VCG Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, priced starting at nearly 16,000 yuan ($2,391) in China, did little to dampen the enthusiasm of Apple fans rushing to buy it. Pre-orders opened at 8 pm on Friday, and the initial allocation quickly sold out. The strong demand underscores the enormous potential and robust purchasing power of China's consumer market, a Chinese expert said. As of press time on Saturday, Apple's official website showed an expected delivery date of January 22, 2027. On Chinese e-commerce platform JD.com, all models in the iPhone Duo series were out of stock, and on Apple's official flagship store on Tmall, an estimated delivery window had been pushed back to January 2, 2027. Meanwhile, the rapid sellout of the initial stock has driven up the "scalper prices" for the iPhone Duo. Global Times asked several sellers on Chinese secondhand trading platform Xianyu and found that the markup on the first batch of iPhone Duo stock is generally over 4,000 yuan. A veteran Apple fan surnamed Tao told the Global Times that he grabbed one on his phone last night, buying the most expensive 2TB version. He said that it was extremely popular on Taobao at the time and sold out in an instant; he succeeded in placing an order on the Apple Store app only after refreshing it repeatedly. At the time of ordering, it showed delivery in early November, but after the order was confirmed, the estimated shipping time was pushed back by a week - roughly November 14 to 21, Tao said. The iPhone Duo, Apple's first flip phone, is on display at one of the company's product launch events on September 9, 2026 Photo: VCG Notably, on Tmall, although the iPhone Duo was not yet available, many consumers had already begun purchasing accessories such as iPhone Duo phone cases. A top-selling iPhone Duo phone case was priced at 192 yuan and showed more than 300 units sold. The strong pre-order demand shows that Chinese consumers still have a strong appetite for high-quality products, and the Chinese consumer market still has enormous potential and tremendous purchasing power, Li Changan, a professor at the Academy of China Open Economy Studies at the University of International Business and Economics, told the Global Times on Saturday. TF International Securities analyst Ming-Chi Kuo noted in an industry survey that assembly shipments of the foldable iPhone in the second half of 2026 will be 7 million to 8 million units, of which third-quarter shipments will be between 500,000 and 1 million units, according to financial news outlet 21jingji.com. The frenzy over the iPhone Duo coincides with Tim Cook's China visit. As executive chairperson of Apple Inc, Cook kicked off the trip on October 11 with an arrival in Guangzhou, capital of South China's Guangdong Province. This marks his first China tour since stepping down as CEO on September 1. In a meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao on Thursday, Cook said that Apple is optimistic about China's development prospects, will further expand its business in China, and is willing to play an active role in promoting the stable and sound development of US-China economic and trade relations, according to the Ministry of Commerce. Global Times

item.title: Takaichi's ritual offering to war shrine further exposes distorted historical view, commitment to neo-militarism: Chinese expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17 11:49:00
Militaristic emblem Illustration: Liu Rui/GT Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Saturday sent a ritual offering to the notorious Yasukuni Shrine under the title of "prime minister," while likely avoiding personally visiting the war shrine out of consideration for relations with China and South Korea, according to Japanese media. Takaichi's latest move further lays bare her distorted view of history and obstinate commitment to pursuing neo-militarism, a Chinese expert said, warning that this would further damage Japan's already strained relations with neighboring countries, including China, South Korea and Russia. Takaichi sent a ritual offering known as masakaki to the war shrine in Tokyo on Saturday, the first day of its three-day autumn festival, under the name "Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi," Japan's Kyodo News reported. The Yasukuni Shrine honors 14 convicted Class-A war criminals responsible for Japan's war of aggression, and is widely considered as a spiritual tool and symbol of Japanese militarism. Lü Chao, an expert on East Asian studies and a professor at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times that Takaichi's latest offering, following several similar moves earlier this year, was likely a political performance aimed at courting far-right forces at home. However, the repeated gestures exposed Takaichi's distorted view of history, which fails to distinguish right from wrong, and laid bare her stubborn commitment to pursuing neo-militarism, Lü said, adding that the latest move risks reinforcing the growing impression that Japan is moving further down the path of neo-militarism and raising concerns about the country's future direction and its relations with regional neighbors. Notably, Takaichi is unlikely to visit the shrine in person during the festival, Kyodo reported, citing a source close to the prime minister. The report suggested she was seeking to avoid further diplomatic friction with China and South Korea. Japanese broadcaster TV Asahi also reported Saturday that Takaichi was expected to refrain from personally visiting the shrine out of consideration for relations with China, which have cooled following her remarks regarding the Taiwan region, as well as Japan's relations with South Korea. Takaichi's reported plan to forgo a personal visit to the war shrine reflects a combination of domestic and international pressures rather than a fundamental change in her position on historical issues, Lü said. Domestically, dissatisfaction has been growing among sections of Japanese society, including business and political circles, over the damage Takaichi's policies have caused to China-Japan relations; internationally, many countries in the Asia Pacific and beyond are increasingly concerned about the resurgence of Japanese militarism, according to Lü. These pressures have apparently made Takaichi wary of personally visiting the shrine in her capacity as prime minister, the expert said. Saturday's offering was the latest in a series of similar gestures by Takaichi this year. During the shrine's spring festival in April, Takaichi sent a masakaki offering and made a monetary offering at her own expense, according to Kyodo News. On August 15, the anniversary of Japan's defeat and surrender in World War II, she again sent a monetary offering to the shrine. She also reportedly performed a remote act of worship toward the war shrine from a parking lot at Tokyo's Nippon Budokan, according to Japanese media reports. China has strongly condemned these moves. On August 15, in response to Takaichi's monetary offering and visits by certain Japanese cabinet members to the war shrine, the Chinese Foreign Ministry issued a statement saying that China strongly deplored Japan's negative moves related to the Yasukuni war shrine, and had lodged serious protests with Japan. "No pretext whatsoever can hide the Japanese politicians' true intention which is to change the verdict on the war criminals, cover up Japan's war crimes, distort the historical facts, and pave the way for accelerating remilitarization," a spokesperson said in the statement. "This is an affront to historical justice, a challenge to the foundational norms of civilization, and a provocation against the postwar international order. Such behaviors have been firmly rejected by the overwhelming majority of the international community," the spokesperson further stated. Takaichi's latest gesture also stands in stark contrast to her recent rhetoric about improving relations with China. In a policy speech to Japan's parliament on October 5, Takaichi described China as an "important neighbor" and expressed her intention to build a stable bilateral relationship, according to Channel News Asia. The remarks attracted attention as a possible signal of Tokyo's willingness to ease tensions after nearly a year of strained relations following Takaichi's erroneous remarks on the Taiwan question. However, Lü dismissed the recent rhetoric as insincere, noting that Takaichi has neither retracted her erroneous remarks on the Taiwan question, which concerns China's core interests, nor offered a formal apology. "Such gestures cannot deceive the Chinese people," Lü said.

item.title: Kindergarten head sentenced to life imprisonment for adding toxic substances to food served to children, staff
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 22:27:00
Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Maiji district, Tianshui, Northwest China's Gansu Province Photo: CCTV A Chinese court on Friday sentenced the head of a kindergarten in Northwest China’s Gansu Province to life imprisonment for instructing staff to add toxic and harmful non-food substances to meals served to children and employees, while five other defendants received prison terms ranging from six to 15 years. The kindergarten’s principal Li Huifang was sentenced to life imprisonment, deprived of political rights for life, and ordered to forfeit 500,000 yuan ($70,000) in personal assets. Zhu Jinglin was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,000 yuan. Four kitchen staff members at the kindergarten – Niu Aiyuan, Wen Yafang, He Xuxia and An Chunling – received prison terms ranging from six to eight years and were also fined. The court found that Li, the de facto person in charge of the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Maiji district, Tianshui, and Zhu, the kindergarten’s executive director, violated national food safety regulations by instructing and arranging for the four kitchen workers to add toxic and harmful non-food substances to food prepared and served to children and staff, causing serious consequences. Six people were arrested in 2025 after deliberately adding toxic lead-containing pigments to children's food, which poisoned 247 pre-schoolers, a government investigation reported on Sunday, according to the Xinhua News Agency in July 2025. The kindergarten principal directed the practice to make food appear more colorful and attractive for marketing, Xinhua reported. The investigation, ordered by Gansu's provincial leadership and involving state environmental and health experts, concluded that cooks at the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten added pigments clearly labeled "inedible" into flour to make corn rolls and date cakes. These pastries have been served to children and staff on a monthly basis since May 2024. Of the kindergarten's 251 children tested, 247 had abnormal blood lead levels (including 14 additional cases identified during follow-up testing), as well as 28 staff members, per Xinhua. Global Times

item.title: Xi stresses prioritizing ecological conservation, pursuing green development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 18:25:00
Photo: Xinhua Chinese President Xi Jinping has emphasized the need to unswervingly follow the path of prioritizing ecological conservation and pursuing green development. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks during an inspection trip on Friday to the city of Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Huangqihai Lake in Ulanqab was once on the verge of drying up due to climate and other impacts. After years of comprehensive conservation, its water body has gradually been restored and expanded. During the inspection trip, Xi visited the Huangqihai Lake nature reserve, where he was briefed on Inner Mongolia's efforts to strengthen ecological conservation, and inspected the lake's shoreline and mudflats and observed birds inhabiting the area. He stressed the need to fully implement the country's wetland protection law, firmly uphold ecological red lines, and safeguard biodiversity. For degraded wetland ecosystems, he called for giving priority to natural restoration, supplemented by human intervention, and carrying out restoration in a scientific and sound manner. Xi visited Chahar High Tech Development Zone in Ulanqab, and learned about Inner Mongolia's progress in advancing the construction of a hub for the "East Data, West Computing" project and the development of the green computing power industry. Noting that implementing the "East Data, West Computing" project and building a national integrated computing power network is an important decision made by the CPC Central Committee, Xi stressed the need to ensure the efficient operation of completed projects and finish the construction of follow-up projects on schedule. He called on all parties to earnestly implement the requirements for efficient, green and safe development, actively promote the development of the green computing power industry, and make greater contributions to building Digital China and developing new quality productive forces. Xi also viewed displays of local agricultural and livestock specialties, encouraging local authorities to better align production with sales to help farmers and herders increase their incomes. item.title: No bullying the small, no blackmail by the small: China's South China Sea rule
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 18:11:00
Philippines South China Sea Illustration: Liu Xidan/Global Times Recent remarks by Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan have been portrayed in Manila as a threat. In fact, they restate a consistent Chinese position: firm defense of territorial sovereignty and maritime rights, together with a preference for peace, restraint and managing differences through direct dialogue. In the South China Sea, China will not use its size to bully the small, nor allow the Philippines to use its smallness to blackmail the strong. China’s approach to territorial and maritime disputes has remained stable for decades. It safeguards its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights while consistently advocating peaceful settlement through bilateral negotiation and consultation. This principle applies not only to the South China Sea but also to other territorial and maritime questions involving its neighbors. The disputes between China and the Philippines have a long history. China maintains that they stem primarily from the Philippines’ occupation of eight features in China’s Nansha Islands beginning in the 1970s and its subsequent claim over Huangyan Island. Overlapping maritime claims also emerged as the international law of the sea developed. Successive Philippine administrations have repeatedly taken actions that have aggravated tensions, including arrests of fishermen from the Chinese mainland and Taiwan, and the unilateral initiation of the South China Sea arbitration case, which China opposed as contrary to prior bilateral understandings and the principle of state consent. China regards its responses to infringement and provocation as legitimate measures to defend its rights. The equality of states under the United Nations Charter and general international law does not give any country a free hand to manufacture incidents at sea. Where a state has illegally occupied another state’s territory, the latter retains, in principle, the right of self-defense. China has exercised considerable restraint, prioritizing regional stability and preserving space for dialogue. That restraint should not be mistaken for the absence of limits. The disparity in national strength, particularly maritime capabilities, between China and the Philippines is an objective fact. Manila cannot expect its repeated provocations, public smearing, and the suspension of military communication channels to be met indefinitely with silence. China has treated the Philippines as an equal neighbor, but restraint is not unlimited. Effective management of maritime differences depends substantially on whether the Philippine government can restrain its military and coast guard. Persistent difficulties in bilateral relations serve neither country’s interests and are particularly damaging to the Philippines’ development. Regional countries should jointly safeguard the region’s hard-won peace and development. Whenever the two sides have moved toward dialogue, certain forces within the Philippines, particularly its military and coast guard, have manufactured incidents to disrupt progress. These forces appear driven less by public welfare than by external powers’ preferences and their own political or institutional interests. If Manila calls for dialogue while allowing these forces to create friction and stoke anti-China sentiment, bilateral communication mechanisms will struggle to function. China and the Philippines are permanent neighbors. Maritime disputes do not change this geographic reality. External military equipment and joint military exercises cannot reverse the regional balance of power. Nor can repeated invocations of a “China threat” narrative resolve the Philippines’ domestic development challenges. Manila may believe that militarization and maritime incidents demonstrate its value as a “frontline platform” for the US and other Western countries, securing stronger security guarantees and economic benefits. Such expectations overlook external powers’ independent strategic calculations. External powers may provide equipment and diplomatic backing while using the Philippines’ geographic location to strengthen their military posture. Their support does not guarantee a willingness to bear the costs of escalation. If a crisis spirals out of control, distant powers can reduce their involvement, leaving the Philippines to face the consequences. History offers repeated warnings about tying national security to another country’s strategic agenda. Manila should weigh that risk carefully. China-Philippines relations stand at a crossroads. Continued tolerance of maritime provocations will invite bolder moves and further damage bilateral ties. The immediate priority for the Marcos government should be to restrain adventurist impulses within its military and coast guard, halt provocations and information operations directed against China, and return to bilateral dialogue and consultation. Only sustained dialogue, supported by restraint and consistent action, can manage differences and stabilize ties. The author is director of the Research Center for International and Regional Studies at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies. opinion@globaltimes.com.cn

item.title: Chinese navy hospital ship arrives in Cote d'Ivoire on medical mission
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 10:56:00
Local honor guards welcome the Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark upon its arrival in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire, Oct. 14, 2026. Auspicious Ark arrived in Abidjan, the economic capital of Cote d'Ivoire, on Wednesday to begin a friendly visit and provide medical services, marking the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the country. The hospital ship, which is carrying out Mission Harmony-2026, docked at Abidjan at about 10:00 a.m. local time (1000 GMT). (Photo by Yvan Sonh/Xinhua) The Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark arrived in Abidjan, the economic capital of Cote d'Ivoire, on Wednesday to begin a friendly visit and provide medical services, marking the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the country. The hospital ship, which is carrying out Mission Harmony-2026, docked at Abidjan at about 10:00 a.m. local time (1000 GMT). Ivorian military and government officials, China's ambassador to Cote d'Ivoire, the defense attache and embassy staff, as well as representatives of the Chinese community and Chinese enterprises welcomed the ship at the port. On board, Chinese naval personnel and civilian staff stood in formation and waved to the welcoming crowd at the port. At the welcoming ceremony, local residents held banners and waved the national flags of China and Cote d'Ivoire to welcome the Chinese naval hospital ship. After the ceremony, the Chief of Staff of the Ivorian Navy boarded the Auspicious Ark and toured the hospital ship. During the seven-day visit, the hospital ship will provide medical treatment for local patients aboard the vessel, while medical personnel will visit the Abidjan Military Hospital and a local university, among other places, for medical exchanges and medical services. The mission will also organize a deck reception to strengthen friendship and mutual trust with the Ivorian side. item.title: Why has 'China Haul' become new buzzword on social media worldwide?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 09:37:00
Foreign tourists buy handheld camera equipment at a flagship store of DJI in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, June 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Liang Xu) More and more foreign visitors are arriving in China with empty suitcases and returning home with bags full of Chinese goods. What is behind this trend? British YouTuber Elliot Page offered a glimpse of the appeal with a shopping vlog filmed in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province. Exploring Chinese sportswear brands such as Li-Ning and Anta, Page was impressed not only by their affordability, but also by their design and quality. Sportswear is just the tip of the iceberg. As "China Haul" gains traction on social media worldwide, an increasing number of international visitors are traveling to China not only to explore its attractions, but also to discover and shop for products that catch their eye. In the first seven months of 2026, people from overseas spent 263.6 billion yuan (about 39 billion U.S. dollars) in China, an increase of 27.8 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Commerce. What is drawing international consumers to Chinese goods? The growing appeal of homegrown Chinese brands is giving international consumers more reasons to take notice. "Chinese products, like clothes, accessories and daily necessities, are not only competitively priced, but also feature trendy designs that are hard to find in stores in my home country," said Carlos Alvarado, an international student from Guatemala, now a seasoned shopper in China. An increasingly visitor-friendly shopping environment is making it easier for international tourists to spend in China. Visa-free entry arrangements and expanded departure tax refund services have further enhanced the country's appeal as a shopping destination. From sprawling shopping malls and efficient delivery services to delivery robots that bring orders right to hotel doors, China offers a seamless shopping experience that lowers the barriers for foreign visitors. "Foreign tourists now account for 30 percent of our daily customer flow," said Zhou Man, manager of a Xiaomi store in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province. Chinese cultural products are broadening the appeal of shopping in China, giving visitors more opportunities to connect purchases with the stories and creativity behind them. From globally popular designer toys such as Labubu to the animated blockbuster Ne Zha 2, Chinese cultural products are capturing international attention. As international audiences become more familiar with Chinese cultural creations, shopping in China can offer another way to discover the country's contemporary culture and everyday life. China Haul, at its core, reflects a simple shift: foreign visitors are discovering China's global appeal firsthand, exploring its products and brands for themselves rather than relying on secondhand impressions. By sharing their shopping finds online, they are introducing the world to a more diverse and appealing side of China.

item.title: 'Forced labor' in Xinjiang's salmon industry, too? The New York Times has lost it: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 23:44:00
A salmon farm in Nilka County, Ili Kazak Autonomous Prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Photo: VCG In their attacks on Xinjiang-related issues, some Western media outlets are still deliberately presenting themselves as "objective and fair," but the signs of preconceived bias and a narrative assembled to fit a predetermined agenda are all too clear. Ultimately, no amount of smearing by US media can erase Xinjiang's economic and social development, nor can it stop people of all ethnic groups at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains from striving for a better life. Recently, The New York Times published a purported in-depth investigative report about the fish farming industry. The article adopts the posture of a "neutral" investigation, citing global research and evidence from multiple sources. It ranges from Peruvian fishing vessels and fishmeal processing plants to offshore aquaculture pens in Norway. Yet in the second half of the article, the focus takes a sharp turn toward the salmon industry in Northwest China's Xinjiang, devoting extensive coverage to recycling familiar allegations such as "forced labor." Read closely, the report reveals a familiar pattern: In their attacks on Xinjiang-related issues, some Western media outlets are still deliberately presenting themselves as "objective and fair," but the signs of preconceived bias and a narrative assembled to fit a predetermined agenda are all too clear. The report offers no evidence from firsthand interviews to support its claims about Xinjiang. Instead, it pieced together much of its narrative from vague attributions with phrases such as "claim," "accuse," and "most likely." By using documented problems in the seafood industry in other parts of the world to shape readers' perceptions in the first half, the article encourages them to assume that the claims made in the second half are equally well substantiated. However, the report provides no solid evidence that similar problems exist in Xinjiang, while packaging subjective speculation as so-called "investigative findings." Such journalistic practices run directly counter to the most basic standards of media credibility. Why are US media outlets willing to lose their credibility just to push out similar fake reports? The real aim, it would appear, is to lend support to Washington's unilateral sanctions targeting Xinjiang. From cotton and tomatoes to sunflower seeds and dumplings, and from solar photovoltaics to polysilicon, the pattern remains the same, with the focus now shifting to Xinjiang's cold-water fish industry: Any competitive industry that benefits Xinjiang's local communities is targeted with the "human rights" cudgel, as negative media coverage is paired with unilateral sanctions to suppress Chinese competitive industries and contain development in China's western regions. It's important to point out that what these sanctions are really aimed at is the employment and development rights of people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang. In fact, Xinjiang's salmon industry is a prime example of how local resources can be harnessed to turn geographical disadvantages into drivers of development. It is also a tangible achievement of China's campaign to develop its western regions in the new era. Nilka County in the Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture benefits from glacial meltwater flowing down from the Tianshan Mountains. The water remains cold and rich in dissolved oxygen throughout the year, and its excellent quality provides exceptional natural conditions for cold-water fish farming. Technologies such as automated feeding, underwater cleaning robots, and semi-closed recirculating aquaculture systems help minimize pollution, while uneaten feed and fish waste can be processed into organic fertilizer. The farming process emphasizes raising fish without medication and at low stocking densities. Companies in the industry have also obtained multiple international food safety certifications. Their products serve the domestic market and are exported to countries across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. They have even gained access to Singapore, a market known for its stringent food standards. Turning desert landscapes into productive fisheries and snow-capped mountains into a source of premium seafood is an industrial success achieved through Chinese ingenuity and hard work. The benefits to people's livelihoods, brought about by industrial development, are being tangibly enjoyed by the people of all ethnic groups. Under a model that combines leading enterprises, employment in industrial parks and social security, some farming and herding families whose livelihoods have revolved around pastoralism for generations have moved into companies and become industrial workers, earning stable wages. Some herders also receive dividends through equity investments. Many young people have chosen to return to their hometowns for work closer to home. The salmon industry has also spurred the growth of fish-themed agritourism, specialty restaurants, rural tourism, and related businesses, opening up additional sources of income and giving fresh impetus to rural vitalization. These concrete, visible improvements in people's lives stand in stark contrast to the falsehoods propagated by some Western media outlets. Ultimately, no amount of smearing by US media can erase Xinjiang's economic and social development, nor can it stop people of all ethnic groups at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains from striving for a better life. It is hoped that some Western media outlets that pride themselves on being "fair and objective" will drop their self-deceptive tactics and go to Xinjiang to see the real production scenes for themselves, listen to workers on the ground describe their own experiences, and gain a firsthand understanding of what human rights really mean to the people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang - and what rights they genuinely enjoy and deserve to have respected.

item.title: Why Takaichi's remarks about nuclear-powered submarines are so dangerous
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 21:59:00
Demonstrators stage a rally before the Diet against the Japanese government's nuclear policies in Tokyo, Japan, on November 21, 2025. Protesters also call on the government to join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. Photo: VCG With her parliamentary remarks, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has pried open a crack in the thickest seal guarding Japan's postwar taboos on military use of nuclear energy. According to Japan's Kyodo News, Takaichi stated during a session of the House of Representatives Budget Committee that in response to the "increased military activity by its neighbors," the Japanese government will "seriously consider" the possibility of Japan Self-Defense Forces (SDF) introducing nuclear-powered submarines. Sources reportedly indicate Tokyo intends to include this option when updating its key documents on defense and security later this year. The phrase "seriously consider" does not indicate prudence, but rather serves as a prelude. While citing "limited intelligence-gathering and surveillance capabilities in the Pacific," Takaichi also singled out nuclear-powered submarine developments in Australia and South Korea - a rhetorical maneuver: She frames Japan as a "passive follower," portrays military expansion as a "defensive necessity," and casts taboo-breaking moves as a "regional trend." Her goal is to embed nuclear-powered submarines in this year's revised security and defense documents, turning a once-forbidden option into a "future initiative" in official policy texts. This is dangerous. Successive Japanese cabinets have long barred the military use of nuclear energy under the Atomic Energy Basic Law, enacted in 1955, which stipulates the peaceful use of nuclear power. In 1965, the Japanese government issued an explicit interpretation prohibiting nuclear energy from being used as propulsion for SDF vessels - an interpretation that has remained in force to this day. "Now, Takaichi's remarks on considering the introduction of nuclear‑powered submarines mark a major conceptual breach of Japan's Atomic Energy Basic Law and the long‑standing Three Non‑Nuclear Principles it underpins," said Lü Yaodong, research fellow at the Institute of Japanese Studies, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. He noted that this was not a spur-of-the-moment statement, but rather an intentional, aggressive step aligned with the revision of three security documents scheduled for this year, a move with significant timing implications. The proposal to introduce nuclear-powered submarines is intended to lay the groundwork for provisions in the revised security documents, push for the inclusion of nuclear-powered submarines in Japan's medium- and long-term defense plans, and pave the way for the further undermining of the Three Non-Nuclear Principles. "Japan is using nuclear-powered submarines as a breakthrough point to challenge the nuclear taboo established after World War II; this is a very dangerous shift," Lü said. In fact, elevating nuclear-powered submarines from a taboo topic to a top-tier policy agenda is a major step in Japan's years-long, incremental process of breaking through postwar military constraints. Zhou Yongsheng, professor at the China Foreign Affairs University, said submarines are inherently offensive platforms for open-ocean operations; equipping them with nuclear propulsion is not merely a "conventional equipment upgrade," but a crucial step toward military nuclear capability. Takaichi's decision to raise this issue in the legislative arena of the House of Representatives had a very clear purpose: to publicly build momentum, secure lawmakers' support, and pave the way for subsequent policy and legislative amendments, according to Zhou. Zhou further pointed out that Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles prohibit the manufacture, possession and introduction of nuclear weapons. A nuclear submarine can be understood as "half a nuclear weapon": Although it is not a full-fledged nuclear bomb, the combination of nuclear propulsion and an offensive submarine platform will effectively introduce military nuclear propulsion capabilities into the SDF. Even more serious is the chain reaction. "Once the Pandora's box of introducing nuclear-powered submarines is opened, it will set a strongly negative precedent and trigger a chain reaction of regional arms races. If this comes to pass, it will cast a shadow over the global nuclear non-proliferation regime," Zhou warned. Today, politicians in Tokyo speak of "seriously considering" this matter as if it were no big deal, but history will not treat it lightly: When nuclear-powered submarines go from being a taboo to a legislative proposal, Japan is not merely revising an ordinary policy, but tearing off the seal on the very aspect of the postwar order that should never be touched.
